title: Investigate holding the state read-lock across the whole marshal
description:
`Marshal` in `go/sync.go:77` takes the state's `Locker` (an `RLock` when the struct exposes `RLocker`) and holds it for the entire `json.Marshal` of the state struct.

## Sizes

At the profiled state size that is **341,817 bytes** serialised under the lock, ~3 ms of marshal on this hardware (14.8% of process CPU / 124.05 MB of the 460.95 MB allocated per 30 s), repeated ~3.7x/sec. So the application's state mutex is held for roughly **1% of wall-clock**, in ~3 ms blocks, purely for serialisation.

## Why it may not be worth changing

A consistent snapshot genuinely requires the lock, and 3 ms x 3.7/sec is not obviously hurting anything measured so far — no lock contention showed up in the production profile. Tasks 2 and 3 also cut the number of marshals directly.

## What to actually do

Measure first: add a contention benchmark (writers mutating state while pushes run) to the task-1 harness and see whether writer latency is affected at 342 KB. Only if it is, consider double-buffering — marshal into a scratch buffer from a cheap copy, or let the application supply a pre-serialised snapshot — and weigh that against the extra copy.

Do not land a speculative fix here. This is the one item on the list without evidence of real-world harm.

## Investigation result (2026-08-10)

Added a deterministic 341,817-byte lock-contention benchmark using the real Marshal/RLocker path. Uncontended writer acquisition averaged about 52–59 ns (p50 40 ns). A writer proven queued before marshal began waited about 4 ms at p50, approximately the full marshal duration; p95 was roughly 5–8 ms depending on scheduler configuration.

This is conditional worst-case latency, not collision frequency. The profiled workload held the read lock for roughly 1% of wall time and showed no production contention. The measurement therefore does not justify speculative double-buffering or changing the snapshot consistency contract. Commit: 41c5bad.
